content: Cosmochemistry focuses on understanding the origin and evolution of chemical elements and their isotopes, particularly within the context of the Solar System. The term cosmochemistry was introduced by Harold Urey. This field is closely related to astrochemistry, which involves the study of chemical elements in other regions of our galaxy and beyond, and astrophysics, which examines the physical processes occurring in stars, supernovae, and within our Solar System that can lead to chemical and isotopic transformations. Additionally, cosmochemistry is a significant subdiscipline of planetary science. A key aspect of cosmochemistry involves the direct analysis of physical samples in Earth-based laboratories. These samples are often meteorites and micrometeorites, which may include material originating from the Moon, Mars, various asteroids, and potentially comets. Some of these samples have been retrieved through manned and robotic lunar missions. Other notable materials studied by cosmochemists include microscopic particles from Comet Wild 2, which were returned to Earth in 2006 by NASA's Stardust mission, and solar wind samples collected by NASA's Genesis mission and brought back in 2004. Among the most unique and scientifically valuable samples are presolar grains, which are microscopic particles embedded in certain primitive chondritic meteorites. These grains formed in other regions of the galaxy before the Solar System came into existence. Similar interstellar dust particles may have been collected by the Stardust mission, although their identification has not yet been confirmed. Since the 1970s, NASA has supported a dedicated research program in cosmochemistry, underscoring the importance of this field in advancing our understanding of the chemical and isotopic history of the Solar System and beyond.
